entities.name: Abu Abd Allah al-Burtuqali Muhammad ibn Muhammad
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Abu Abd Allah al-Burtuqali Muhammad ibn Muhammad (d. 1526) was the second Wattasid Sultan of Morocco, a pivotal figure in the dynasty's consolidation of power during the Medieval period. Born in Fez, he inherited the throne upon the death of his father Abu Abd Allah al-Sheikh Muhammad ibn Yahya in 1504, a transition that marked a critical moment in the establishment of dynastic succession traditions within the Wattasid realm.

During his reign from 1504 to 1526, Muhammad al-Burtuqali presided over a kingdom navigating the complex interplay of religious authority, feudal governance structures, and the expansion of Mediterranean trade networks. The Wattasid dynasty, of which he was a leading representative, played a crucial role in the broader transformation of North African political systems and the geopolitical dynamics that would shape regional power balances throughout the early modern period.

Muhammad al-Burtuqali's rule contributed significantly to the establishment of dynastic legacies and the definition of territorial boundaries that would endure in the Maghreb. His governance reflected the synthesis of classical Islamic thought with contemporary political theory, influencing intellectual currents that resonated across the Mediterranean and contributed to the broader ideological ferment of the Renaissance and Reformation periods in Europe.

Upon his death in 1526, he was succeeded by his son Abu al-Abbas Ahmad ibn Muhammad, ensuring the continuation of Wattasid dynastic authority. His reign exemplifies the Medieval era's complex political landscape, characterized by the tension between monarchical sovereignty and religious legitimacy, feudal obligations, and the emerging importance of commercial networks in shaping statecraft and international relations.
